newsitem.title: CROATIA: Tudjman reappears after 10 days looking better. [CORRECTED 16:00 GMT]
newsitem.headline: Tudjman reappears after 10 days looking better. [CORRECTED 16:00 GMT]

text.p: Croatian President Franjo Tudjman, reportedly suffering from cancer, appeared in public for the first time in 10 days on Friday looking cheerful and more healthy.

Croatian media and Western diplomats speculated this week that the 74-year-old president, who steered Croatia to independence from federal Yugoslavia in 1991, had undergone medical treatment during his unusual absence from view.

Tudjman is said by U.S. sources to have untreatable stomach cancer and diplomats in Croatia said on Wednesday they now believed it was "a matter of months" before he is incapacitated, or possibly dead.
The the ruling Croatian Democratic Union (HDZ) has no obvious candidate to replace Tudjman in case he is unable or unwilling to run in presidential elections due later this year.
Reuters Television footage on Friday showed Tudjman, while still much thinner than three months ago, in apparently better health with rosy cheeks and moving with his old ease.

Speculation about Tudjman's illness, combined with a strange lack of official information, lured a pack of international television crews and photographers on Friday (corrects from Monday) to a protocol meeting at the presidential palace, an event normally covered only by a handful of domestic media.
"What kind of invasion is this?" said Tudjman, who smiled and appeared to be in good spirits, obviously eager to dispel grim reports about his physical condition.

The last appearance of the nationalist leader was on Year's Eve in Zagreb's main square, when state television footage showed him pale and gaunt, heightening speculation that his condition was rapidly deteriorating.

Recent reports in independent media, quoting Croat medical circles, said Tudjman's condition was worse than believed at first in November, when he returned from treatment in the United States, and that he only had a few months to live.
Zagreb weeklies Nacional and Globus quoted doctors as saying Tudjman was receiving daily infusions of blood, nutrients and vitamins to prevent rapid weight loss.
They also said a special suite was being prepared for him at the New Hospital in Zagreb, a former Yugoslav army clinic.

Vjesnik, the main state-run newspaper, dismissed reports that Tudjman was terminally ill, saying he "had normal working obligations in the past few days, with several routine matters of business to attend."
Tudjman had no plans to leave Zagreb and his health had not worsened, it said. He is "feeling very well and is normally carrying out his official duties", it said in an editorial.
Tudjman is expected to deliver a speech to parliament on January 22 announcing constitutional changes, Vjesnik said.
But Vjesnik, which often reflects official government views, said most changes were matters of style and did not involve abolishing the presidential system.

Independent media carried reports in the past few months that the HDZ is planning to change the constitution so that the parliament -- in which they hold the majority till 1999 -- elects the president.
Vjesnik said the constitution, written in 1990 when Croatia was still a part of Yugoslavia, contained linguistically and politically outdated wording which had to be changed.
